The Chronicle of Georgia

Tsereteli's colossal bronze pillars above the Tbilisi Sea — the city's most cinematic sunset viewpoint.

Time needed
1 h
From Tbilisi
14 km · 0:30
Road
Paved
Car needed
Economy class
Season
All year
Entry
free

Sixteen pillars, each about sixteen metres tall, standing on an empty hill. Zurab Tsereteli began this monument in 1985 and it has never been finished, which is part of why the site feels so strange and so cinematic. It rarely appears in printed guidebooks and constantly appears on Instagram.

The lower half of each column carries relief figures of Georgian kings, queens, heroes and poets, from Vakhtang Gorgasali to Shota Rustaveli. The upper half is given to biblical scenes: the Nativity, the Crucifixion, the Resurrection. National history and sacred history meet at the two ends of the same vertical, an idea Tsereteli returned to throughout his career.

From the edge of the hill the view opens over the Tbilisi Sea, the large reservoir that supplies the city, with wind turbines on the ridges and dry steppe hills beyond. The landscape looks nothing like the rest of Tbilisi and rather more like Central Asia.

One practical truth: the place is essentially unmanaged. There is no ticket, no real infrastructure, no lighting after dark, and the concrete platform is cracked in places. That is neither a flaw nor a virtue, simply what it is — and the reason it is often almost empty when you arrive.

Practical advice

Come in the hour before sunset: the columns face west and the bronze catches fire in that light. Do not linger after dark, since there is no lighting and the surfaces are uneven. There is no shade at all in summer and the wind is constant, so bring a hat and water. No toilets, café or ATM on site — the nearest facilities are along the Tbilisi Sea road. An hour is more than enough time here, unless you are photographing.

How to get there from Tbilisi

The monument stands on the northern edge of the city near the western shore of the Tbilisi Sea. From the centre take George Bush Street or the Tbilisi Sea road, roughly 25 to 30 minutes. The last two kilometres are narrow, patched asphalt with potholes, but perfectly passable. Navigation apps sometimes suggest a poor turning, so use the Tbilisi Sea shore road and its upper branch as your reference. Parking is free right at the columns. An economy car copes, though a crossover makes the last stretch more comfortable.
